mean: to accept something as true without checking it
ex: Don't assume the Harbour line is running late just because it rained last night; check the app first.
note: Assume = believe without proof. 'Assume charge' (common in Indian news) means take up a post: 'She assumed charge as collector.'

mean: to decide something is true after thinking about the facts
ex: After checking the meter twice, the electrician could only conclude that the wiring in the old Kolkata flat was faulty.
note: Also means 'to end': 'The meeting concluded at six.' The noun is 'conclusion'; 'jump to conclusions' means decide too fast.

mean: facts or signs that show whether something is true
ex: The CCTV footage was the only evidence that the scooter had been parked outside the chemist's shop in Lucknow.
note: Uncountable: say 'a piece of evidence' or 'a lot of evidence', never 'an evidence' or 'evidences'.

mean: following clear, sensible reasoning
ex: Shifting the wedding to December was the logical choice, since the monsoon would ruin an outdoor mandap in July.
note: Opposite: illogical. 'Logical' is about the reasoning being sound, not about being clever or unemotional.

mean: connected to what is being discussed or done
ex: The interviewer in the Bengaluru office said Arjun's experience as a college cricket captain was relevant to the team-lead role.
note: Often misspelled 'relavant'. The opposite is 'irrelevant', not 'unrelevant'.

mean: to study something closely, part by part, to understand it
ex: The coach asked Shreyas to analyse the video of every ball he got out to this season.
note: British/Indian spelling is 'analyse'; American is 'analyze'. Noun: analysis, plural analyses.

mean: to work something out from the clues you have
ex: From the half-eaten paratha and the open window, Amma could infer that the neighbour's cat had visited the kitchen.
note: The speaker implies (hints); the listener infers (works it out). 'Are you inferring I'm lazy?' is wrong; say 'implying'.

mean: an unfair leaning for or against someone or something
ex: Fans accused the umpire of bias after three close lbw calls all went against the visiting team.
note: The adjective is 'biased': 'a biased report', not 'a bias report'. Confirmation bias = noticing only what supports what you already believe.

mean: the situation or surrounding facts that explain something
ex: Taken out of context, Chachaji's joke in the family WhatsApp group sounded far ruder than he meant it.
note: 'Quoted out of context' is a common trick: a line cut from what came before it can seem to mean the opposite.

mean: a particular way of seeing or thinking about something
ex: A week on her uncle's farm in Punjab gave Simran a new perspective on why vegetable prices jump.
note: 'Put things in perspective' means judging how important something really is, without exaggerating it.

mean: a likely result, or something suggested without being said directly
ex: Nobody at the Pune startup had thought through the implication of storing customer data on a free server abroad.
note: Often plural for effects: 'the implications of the new rule'. Linked to 'imply', not to 'implicate' (show someone is involved in a crime).

mean: based on facts, not on personal feelings or opinions
ex: The editor told the new reporter to stay objective while covering the dispute between the two housing societies.
note: Opposite: subjective. As a noun, 'objective' means a goal: 'the objective of this meeting'.

mean: an idea you accept as true and build an argument or plan on
ex: The whole plan rested on the premise that the new metro line would open before Diwali, and it didn't.
note: Don't mix with 'premises', which means a building and its land: 'No smoking on the premises.'

mean: a small but important difference in meaning or feeling
ex: Good translators catch every nuance of a Ghalib couplet.
note: A 'nuanced view' sees more than one side of a question.

mean: seeming likely to be true or reasonable
ex: Rohan's excuse that the Delhi metro was stuck in a tunnel for an hour sounded plausible, so the teacher let him in.
note: Plausible is not the same as true: it only seems likely. Good liars tell very plausible stories.

mean: clear, with all its parts fitting together sensibly
ex: After two sleepless nights before the board exam, Ananya could barely write a coherent answer.
note: Opposite: incoherent. 'Coherent' is about ideas fitting together; 'cohesive' is about a group sticking together.

mean: a link where two things tend to rise or fall together
ex: The study found a correlation between ice-cream sales and drownings in Goa, but summer heat was driving both.
note: Correlation is not causation: two things moving together does not prove one causes the other.

mean: a common belief or step in reasoning that is wrong
ex: It is a fallacy that a student who scores low in the Class 10 boards cannot do well in life.
note: In logic, a fallacy is a faulty step in an argument (like a straw man), even if the conclusion happens to be true.

mean: an idea that might explain something, which still has to be tested
ex: Dr Iyer's hypothesis was that the dengue cases came from water lying in the construction site's open tanks.
note: Plural: hypotheses (high-POTH-uh-seez). A hypothesis is still to be tested; a scientific theory has been tested many times.

mean: very careful and strict, checking every detail
ex: Every new medicine must pass rigorous trials before doctors at a Chennai hospital can prescribe it.
note: Don't confuse with 'vigorous' (full of energy). A rigorous check is exact; a vigorous one is energetic.

mean: based on what is seen or tested, not only on theory
ex: To check the farmers' belief that neem spray protects cotton, the agriculture college in Nagpur collected empirical data from fifty fields.
note: Opposite: theoretical. 'Empirical evidence' means evidence from observation or experiment, not from argument alone.

mean: something that seems impossible or self-contradicting but may still be true
ex: It is a paradox that Cherrapunji, one of the wettest places on earth, runs short of drinking water in winter.
note: 'Paradoxically' is a useful sentence opener: 'Paradoxically, building more roads can create more traffic.'

mean: a sharp split between two opposite things or ideas
ex: The TV panel fell into a false dichotomy: either build the highway or save the forest, with nothing in between.
note: A 'false dichotomy' pretends only two options exist. Don't use 'dichotomy' just to mean any 'difference'.

mean: a simple rule of thumb that helps you decide quickly
ex: Nani's heuristic for buying mangoes at Crawford Market was simple: smell the stalk end before you pay.
note: Heuristics save time but can mislead; many biases are heuristics gone wrong. Also an adjective: 'a heuristic approach'.

mean: saying the same thing twice in different words, adding nothing
ex: The Hyderabad ad agency dropped the slogan 'new innovation' after the client pointed out the tautology.
note: Common slips: 'return back', 'repeat again', 'PIN number', 'free gift'. Just say 'return', 'repeat', 'PIN', 'gift'.
